These are in allow.txt and are being ignored. A rule that was silently dropped is a rule you think is protecting you.
Rules are pinned: they survive a profile switch, a list update and a reset. They are compiled into the index at the next build.
This runs the same matcher netd runs, against the index the device is serving right now — not a guess about it.
Enter a host name to check.
The resolver answers this name from the index instead of the network, so nothing on the device reaches it.
Nothing in this index matches this name. DNS for it resolves normally.
The index could not be read, so there is no verdict to give. This is not the same as “not blocked”.
The matcher does not look at this name at all — an address literal, a single label, or a reserved suffix such as .local. The resolver passes it through untouched.
Source: group %1$d (the manifest for this index generation is missing, so it has no name)
Why this one is not in the lists

The upstream lists deliberately leave the apex of doubleclick.net, googleadservices.com and graph.facebook.com unblocked and block their specific ad subdomains instead — blocking the apex breaks Google sign-in, Play billing and Facebook login in apps that use them. google-analytics.com is present and is blocked. So “this domain is not blocked” here is a decision by the list author, not a broken filter.

%1$s is one of the names the upstream lists leave alone on purpose: they block its ad subdomains and leave the apex resolvable, because blocking it breaks sign-in and billing. This is not a sign that filtering has stopped.
If you think filtering has stopped, the Home screen measures it. This screen only reads the index.
There is no index on this device yet, so there is nothing to ask. Run an update first.
netd reads the calling app\'s uid from the socket, so an exemption here is exact rather than a guess about which app is in the foreground.
Exempt — nothing is blocked for this app
Shares a uid with %1$d other apps; exempting it exempts all of them.
Nullroute filters itself on purpose. The Home screen proves filtering is live by resolving its own probe name, so an exemption here would make a healthy device report “not filtering”.
No installed package claims this uid any more. The exemption is still live in the control page; switching it off is how you clear it.
The control page is not mapped, so per-app policy cannot be changed. Diagnostics has the reason.
Applied. It takes effect on this app\'s next DNS query.
There is no “strict” setting. The resolver only implements an exemption, and a switch that changed nothing would be worse than no switch.
Independent of the profile. Each row says what turning it on costs, because two of them are switches that read backwards.
ON stops allowing these domains and lets the blocklists block them.
Turning this on blocks the endpoints your own VPN or private DNS uses. If you use either, they will stop connecting and the cause will not be obvious.
Turning this on lets the blocklists block device-fingerprinting hosts. Banking and payment apps are built on them: expect logins that spin forever or refuse to complete.
Turning this on lets the blocklists block deferred deep-link hosts. Delivery, ride-hailing and referral flows use them: expect onboarding loops and links that open the wrong screen.
Changes are compiled in at the next build. Until then the index is unchanged.
The shipped profile is read-only, so your edits are stored as an overlay. An OTA can change what this profile means without discarding them.
A list\'s own syntax cannot tell the two apart — HaGeZi ships the same 1,604 domains as both a blocklist and an allowlist — so this has to be recorded, not sniffed.
